classification.difficultyReason: Requires identifying an invariant in the alternating board colours and using it to rule out every domino covering.

content.prompt: A standard $8\times8$ chessboard has two diagonally opposite corners removed, leaving 62 squares. Is it possible to place 31 dominoes of size $2\times1$ so as to cover all of the remaining squares?

spec.sourceRegion: Right column, question 14, chessboard beneath the stem.
spec.description: Eight aligned rows and columns with alternating black and red squares; upper-left and lower-right corners are absent and shown as rotated detached red squares.
spec.mathematics: The two removed corners have the same colour. The remaining board has 32 black squares and 30 red squares. Every edge-adjacent pair contains one square of each colour.
spec.answerVisibility: The question diagram preserves only the supplied board and detached corners; no counts or solution annotations are printed.

inlines.text: The board has 32 black and 30 red squares, but each domino covers one of each colour.

answer.worked:
An intact board has 32 squares of each colour. Both removed corners are red, leaving 32 black squares and 30 red squares.

Every $2\times1$ domino covers two adjacent squares, one black and one red. Therefore, 31 dominoes would cover 31 squares of each colour. The remaining board has unequal colour counts, so a covering is impossible.
